2490419,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.1.1,1967-05-19,51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f,ca.m.6889,Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,MEETING IN MONTREAL OF TJ.S.-CANADA MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE,,,"Mr. Speaker, the joint Canada-United States ministerial committee on trade and economic affairs which was established in November, 1953 normally meets every year, alternately in Canada and the United States. It has now been agreed that the committee, which held its last meeting in Washington on March 4, 1966, will meet again from June 20 to June 22 in Montreal. The United States representatives will be the guests of the Canadian government at Expo '67 on June 20.

The Canadian delegation is chaired by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and normally includes the Ministers of Trade and Commerce, Finance, Industry, Energy, Mines and Resources, and Agriculture. The United States delegation is normally led by the Secretary of State and generally includes the Secretaries of the Treasury, Agriculture, Commerce and the Interior.

As in the past this meeting will provide a valuable opportunity for ministers of both countries to review economic and trade questions of common interest and concern. Canadian ministers look forward to welcoming their United States colleagues to Montreal at Expo '67 and to having useful discussiens with them.

,Liberal,,Lester Bowles Pearson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f&Language=E&Section=ALL

2490462,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.12.5.1.2,1967-05-19,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,TRANSPORT AND COMMUNICATIONS,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,VIET NAM-OPPORTUNITY FOR EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN VIEWPOINT,Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Prime Minister whether he would give consideration to providing an opportunity at once for the introduction in this house of a resolution regarding the Viet Nam situation, and in particular whether such a resolution would call upon the United States to discontinue bombing or, if not, to restrict it to communication roads.

Since yesterday the report is that for the first time in the demilitarized zone there has been warfare, or warfare is expected, because of the presence of both North Vietnamese and the Americans in that area. This adds a very sobering thought as to the possibilities which may arise through escalation of this type.

In view of the further serious developments in that area in the last 24 hours and the necessity of something being done by Canada to make clear the viewpoint held by the elected representatives in parliament, would the Prime Minister not now give an assurance that provision will be made for debate on such a resolution to bring clearly to the notice of the United States and the world our view on such matters before it may become too late?

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
2490463,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.12.5.1.3,1967-05-19,51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f,ca.m.6889,Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,TRANSPORT AND COMMUNICATIONS,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,VIET NAM-OPPORTUNITY FOR EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN VIEWPOINT,Consideration of the suggestion made by the right hon. gentleman yesterday is not yet completed. When it is, I shall be glad to make an announcement to the house at as early a date as possible.

As far as the reference to the demilitarized zone is concerned, it is well known, of course, that the neutrality of that zone has been violated more than once over the years. It has also been stated by this government and by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, specifically I think on April 11, that we would consider it regrettable if that zone were used as a base for operations by troops of either 27053-271

,Liberal,,Lester Bowles Pearson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f&Language=E&Section=ALL

House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.,TRANSPORT AND COMMUNICATIONS,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,VIET NAM-OPPORTUNITY FOR EXPRESSION OF CANADIAN VIEWPOINT,A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. ,New Democratic Party,,Stanley Howard Knowles,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78&Language=E&Section=ALL

2490482,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.14.2.1.5,1967-05-19,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,FINANCE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SITUATION,The member nations of the peace keeping force yesterday met with the Secretary General of the United Nations for the second time. He informed them that as the result of a demand made on the commander of the force by the foreign minister of the U.A.R. he had no alternative but to accept the demand that the United Nations emergency force withdraw and that it vacate U.A.R. territory.

At this meeting the ambassador of Canada pointed out that it was the view of the Canadian government that such a decision could only be taken by the security council or the general assembly, and in this case by the general assembly since the force had been established by that body. However, all members contributing to the force did not and do not share this juridical interpretation of the assembly's authority.

It may be recalled that not only did the present Prime Minister, as secretary of state for external affairs in 1957, establish the government's position that the authority of the assembly was required before the force could be disbanded, but this position likewise was taken by the government of my right hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition in June of 1967, when the Canadian ambassador informed the then secretary general that there could be no withdrawal of the force except on the authority of the general assembly.

2490484,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.14.2.1.7,1967-05-19,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,FINANCE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SITUATION,In June of 1960, when Ambassador Ritchie went to the then secretary general, Dag Hammarskjold, and informed him that the Canadian government could not agree that there should be any withdrawal of the force without the authority of the general assembly.

The Canadian ambassador to the United Nations will be seeing the Secretary General today at noon. I would hope there would be a meeting of the security council as quickly as possible, when this body might take into account the serious situation which has developed. Yesterday I had a talk with the United Arab Republic ambassador, who informed me of the decision of his government. I in turn indicated what was our view as to the authority of the general assembly. Likewise I saw the ambassador of Israel. Before there was a formal indication by the Secretary General that the force had been disbanded I made the suggestion that Israel might give consideration to inviting the force to occupy its territory so the force might continue in being.

In any event, consultations are continuing among the governments concerned at the United Nations and in Ottawa as well as in other capitals. The situation I believe is one which must be scrutinized with the greatest care. The situation now is that the forces of the U.A.R. are occupying the posts along the armistice line formerly occupied by the United Nations patrol which carried on surveillance along the armistice line of 175 miles. So the U.A.R. and Israeli forces now are confronting one another.

In this situation 1 would hope that all countries concerned would exercise the greatest moderation, particularly in view of the fact that the Secretary General, supported by some countries members of the United Nations force, has taken the position that the force now is no longer in being. The Secretary General will report to the United Nations general assembly today on the action he has taken. There will be an opportunity, of course, for the Canadian government and others to state their position about the withdrawal of the force which, however now regrettably must be regarded as officially disbanded.

2490536,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.18.1.2,1967-05-19,931e9f4e-5057-4773-869e-1d9abdb3b9cc,ca.m.2051,Mr. Rene Emard (Vaudreuil-Soulanges):,,SPEECH FROM THE THRONE,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,"Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue my comments on the new capitalist doctrine set forth by Kelso and Adler in Le manifeste capitaliste and The New Capitalists.

In his work Kelso dwells particularly on measures to give the individual a greater share of the capital. According to him, to the widely applied profit-sharing system should be added the various pension plans most commonly in use today. He adds that the practice of deducting contributions to various plans, such as profit-sharing plans-and particularly bonuses in the form of shares-from the taxable income could be used to bring about a transition from our mixed economy to pure capitalism. This transition, continues the author, could take place without any change in income tax rates. According to Mr. Kelso's theory, if profit-sharing plans are well conceived, after a few years of work, the worker becomes the owner of a substantial portion of capital. Therefore, these plans will help change our economy into a capitalistic one. If joint stock companies established on a sound basis were obliged to pay to their shareholders all the income created by their capital, profit-sharing plans would become much more effective. In fact, the amounts of money paid to the workers could be used to buy shares in those joint stock companies. According to Mr. Kelso, the concept of profit sharing should not be tied to the idea of retirement as it is now in an economy which is concerned with the idea of full employment. A greater participation in capital ownership, therefore in the production of wealth, will provide the worker with an income which will not only provide him with a livelihood when he stops working, but also which
The Address-Mr. Emard

According to Mr. Kelso, since capital equipment has obviously become the main factor in the production of wealth, the economic system must be revised to spread the ownership of capital equipment to the entire population. Too many of our political leaders, industrialists, economists say we lack the capital to build our country. Many of them add that even if we had the capital, we would not have the guts to use it. But Mr. Kelso feels that we not only have the capacity to produce the required capital, but that we also have the political obligation to do so if we are to remain a strong and independent country.

World capitalism rejects the socialist and classical (non-socialist) theory according to which prosperity can be achieved only by full employment. Such a theory erroneously assumes that the only way man can contribute to production is through his labour. It overlooks the non-human factor of production which is capital and it fails to recognize that capital produces wealth just as labour does, and that capital currently produces the greater part of the total goods and services and that, as technology develops, capital will produce an ever-increasing part in the future. The purpose of pure or universal capitalism is a maximum yield of goods and services with a minimum of labour but with universal participation in production. Participation may come through personal labour or through personal ownership of producing capital, or through both, according to the degree of development of technology or the standard of living being aimed at.

For the author, the word ""universal"" in the expression ""universal capitalism"" has the same meaning as in the expression ""universal suffrage"" and both are closely connected. The political system of universal suffrage has never had an economic equivalent in history. Defective economic institutions have weakened and eliminated the ideals of political democracy and constitutional government, according to Mr. Kelso's conclusions. Our western political heritage has no chance to survive in a nation or in a world where capital is the main source of wealth desired by all but where the majority owns no productive property. Private property, as applied to the factors of production, means that the owner of each factor is entitled to all the wealth or the net yield produced by the property owned.
The practical world in which we are living demands in addition to a theory, practical and efficient means to put theory in action. The

second income plan is a practical plan to achieve a universal capitalist economy. An economy capable of producing whealth at the required rate would have to be at least ten times more productive than that now in existence in Canada, according to Mr. Kelso. The purpose of the plan for a second income is therefore to create that new economy.

Under that economy, newly created capital would be owned first of all by the 90 per cent of families which do not have a large income in the present economy. This new economy would be based on means to increase the integrity of the present right to private property in the existing economy. Mr. Kelso states further that such economy will have logic and symmetry, because it builds up the economic power of all families to consume goods, that is the buying power, thanks to two sources of income, at the same time as it builds up industrial capacity to produce goods.

The instruments of economic transformation suggested by the author fall under four categories: those relating to legacies and to donations inter vivos, in so far as they are affected by federal and provincial fiscal legislation; those respecting corporative policy; the instruments dealing with the financing of capital ownership for company workers and, finally, those relating to the financing of capital ownership for employees other than those of companies.

The purpose of changes in the fiscal policy affecting real estate and tax legislation on donations should be to encourage donations likely to extend private capital ownership by having it benefit a greater number of people. Those legislative measures should discourage blocking of accumulating the most efficient production factor, capital, in foundations the purpose of which is rather vague or obscure but which are tax exempt.
In such foundations, capital is socialized as efficiently as through state confiscation. With regard to corporations, Kelso makes the three following suggestions:

Compel gradually well established companies to pay their shareholders the full amount of their gains, after allowing for the cost of depreciation and operating reserves. To withhold income from capital is no more justifiable than to withhold income from work. If capital produces the greater part of our wealth, and if we want to streamline our economic system by allowing the mass to get

column1: a secondary income in the form of dividends, the private property of both present and new shareholders must be effective.

column2: To provide companies with new sources of financial growth in order to replace internal funds now in use.

column1: If existing capital is used as a warranty in the financing process, then, according to Kelso, there is a better way to achieve the same goal, a method which does not depend on the limits imposed by the savings available for financing the formation of new capital.

This idea is of major importance for the Canadian economy, for it breaks the necessary tie, in conventional finance, between the ownership of existing capital and the right to acquire the ownership of newly constituted capital.

Conventional finance is a method whose results are exactly the contrary of universal capitalism. It is a method of implacable concentration of ownership and of exclusion, from the ownership of capital, of those who do not already possess a substantial amount of money.

On the other hand, the secondary income plan is a method created to allow people, who were born without it, to buy capital, to pay for it with the wealth produced by this capital and, afterwards, to own it and to use it as a source of secondary income.

Finally, Mr. Kelso points out some political advantages of an economic program based upon a second income plan. He says that the tools of that plan are particularly useful at the federal level because their operation is first subject to the control of the monetary system and the credit system which come under the federal government.

That plan is in keeping with the national economic planning, the antitrust policy, the speeding up of economic growth through the simultaneous development of the economic power of the people to consume and their industrial capacity to produce and also with the promotion of industrial peace. At the same time, the purpose of this plan is to maintain among individual citizens a growing economic power resulting from an accelerated industrialization and to extend it throughout the nation. Eventually and ideally, that extension would be universal.

The plan is also intended to reduce drastically and perhaps to remove economic cycles. The Second Revenue Plan will unavoidably show to all Canadians the advantages of a strong Confederation of all provinces. The control of the financial policy by the central 27053-281

In addition, by increasing industrial power, economic independence and prestige of the political and economic leadership of Canada, the plan can narrow down the difference between the power of the United States and Canada.

The plan also portends to show that Canada does not need any foreign financial capital, but that all Canadians must have an opportunity to quickly own as many capital goods as possible. It is through an income increase due to the ownership of capital, rather than an artificial wage increase, that Canada could compete favourably with any other nation, including European and Japanese manufacturers for the American market. The second income plan provides Canadians with the tools which could place their economy among the most important in the world, within a few years. Such an economy, built upon simple principles workable and understandable, could be emulated by that of developing countries. Today, concludes Mr. Kelso, there is no similar model for emerging nations.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people lose a lot of time in academic discussions about reforms which never bring any results. The second income plan presents a practical program, and the least we can do would be to study its potentialities.

Their eloquent words have lifted this debate and launched it on a high plane. I for one was distinctly impressed by the debut each of them made. I know what they had to say has had a profound effect on the direction and course this debate has taken, and I think throughout the life of this session and this parliament their remarks will contribute to the over-all calibre and standard of debate and our participation in the affairs of the nation.

I should now like to address myself to two or three areas of Canadian life that I think are worthy of attention as I avail myself of this opportunity to take part in what is in fact a truly historic debate, because this particular throne speech debate is taking place in our one hundredth birthday year which celebrates confederation.

One of the matters I want to talk about is our presence abroad in the world, particularly our presence across the Pacific ocean in Asia, where one and a half billion people or half the population of the world resides. I had the good fortune and opportunity to spend a brief time in Southeast Asia during February and March, 22 days in all, during which my travelling party visited seven countries. For many of us it was our first glimpse of a huge area of life, endeavour and enterprise, a huge area of human struggle, bordering the Pacific ocean which washes the shores of our own country. It is an area in which our country must take a deep and abiding interest from both a spiritual and economic point of view.

In our travels in that part of the world we found that though we are held in fairly high regard as a nation we have no presence to speak of in Asia. We are held in fairly high regard as a direct result, first, of the presence in Southeast Asia now and in past of certain individuals who have enhanced our country's
! Mr. Sherman.)

name; and second, because of our wheat sales to China, the latter leaving the impression, fortunately for us, that as a country we are more concerned with keeping people from starving than with political divisions. The individuals who have enhanced our name worked chiefly in medical and missionary teams. Also some of our official and quasiofficial diplomats in Asia are held in high regard.

Despite these small evidences that we are not completely unknown-it is true that we may be recognized as existing-we cannot claim that anyone understands us or that we have any political presence in the area. We may not be dismissed as puppets of the United States, but we are hardly considered to have an independent foreign policy. It appears difficult for Asians to understand why we do not recognize or have diplomatic relations with a country to which we sell hundreds of million of dollars worth of wheat every year. A general vacuum exists in feelings toward our country; we have not made ourselves interested or interesting, and as a result little notice is taken of us.

These facts may be directly related to our almost complete lack of representation in the area. In the 15 countries of Southeast Asia with which we have diplomatic relations we maintain five embassies and six trade commissions, some of the latter being accredited to other countries as well as those in which they are located. Nevertheless it is doubtful whether the personnel of those establishments are numerous enough to be of much use to more than one country at a time. In eight of the 15 countries I alluded to we are unrepresented.
The following is the table of our offices and officers, sir:
India: high commission, trade commission.
Pakistan: high commission, trade commission.
Japan:

column1: Malaysia:
(also accredited to Singapore).
Hong Kong: trade commission.
Philippines: trade commission.
Indonesia: consulate.
Viet Nam: ICC commissioner; Laos: ICC commissioner; Cambodia: ICC commissioner; no diplomatic representation.
Thailand: no representation.
Burma: no representation.
Singapore: no representation.
Korea: no representation.
Formosa: no representation.
Mainland China is not included, and by Korea I mean South Korea. Forgetting for a

moment the whys and wherefores of recognizing or not recognizing communist China, the figures show that Canada has a total representation of some 25 foreign service officers in an area where lj billion people live. In our five embassies-one is a consulate-and six trade commissions which are accredited to eight countries we have two dozen persons of officer rank who, in effect, bring Canada to half the world's people. Considering that Canada's major market for wheat is in this area, and considering also the vastly increased political importance of Southeast Asia, we need much greater representation that we presently have.

The nature of our representation only makes the situation worse. This is not to say that our personnel are not doing an excellent job, for from all reports and under all the circumstances they are. But the fact remains that Canada has not one expert on Southeast Asia, not one. The external affairs department prefers not to have experts; it likes to move its people around to widen their knowledge and experience.

Surely such a modus operandi is sadly out of date in 1967, and will be even more out of date in the 1970's when all these nations to which we pay so little attention will be the scene of many struggles that will increasingly involve every nation of the world, our own included. How can we deal effectively with these cultures so different from our own without the modern equivalent of the old China hand? The Department of External Affairs does not offer its applicants any kind of choice in their overseas postings. Probably a person skilled in the ways of Southeast Asia will be sent to Southeast Asia, but not necessarily.

The recruitment of foreign service officers is undertaken at the postgraduate level simply by a series of examinations and interviews. No attempt is made to interest young Canadians in the foreign service of their country. There are no incentives for Canadian university students to undertake studies which will lead them to careers in any particular branch of the foreign service, or to careers in any government branch at all for that matter. There are no resident experts in Ottawa or abroad. Everyone is eligible for everything once he is accepted into the foreign service. Obviously a man who speaks Japanese will not be sent to the Netherlands. Generally, though, we conduct our foreign policy on the career level as we would a liberal arts college. No specialized knowledge is required and very little is gained.
DEBATES
The Address-Mr. Sherman

Complete overhaul of our recruitment system is demanded to ensure a steady flow of interested young people into branches of the service that require expertise. Our ambassador to a country should be not only an excellent person, a good diplomat and a good ambassador; he should also be an expert on that country. In a modern, specialized world we must give direction to our foreign policy by placing in foreign capitals men who know and understand those to whom they are accredited. With a proper and informed flow back of material we may better be able to direct our country's activities abroad.

It is necessary to let young Canadians know about the foreign service as a career, before they choose a career. At the moment, foreign service personnel become so because their fathers did, or because they discover they are qualified after acquiring one or two college degrees. The opportunity is great. Excellent people have been attracted. But the needs have changed. If we think we can get by in Southeast Asia with 25 officers, we are sadly mistaken. If we send anybody but an expert out to increase the complement, we may as well spend the money and the talent elsewhere.

The figures on career officers show that applicants know very little about the jobs they are applying for. Of 800 applicants for career officer posts in 1966, only 170 qualified to write the entrance exams. Four hundred were not even sufficiently qualified or interested to be interviewed. Sixty were accepted. Undoubtedly the standards are high, but today the potential ambassador needs more specialized knowledge than he ever needed before. His specialization must begin at the graduate level, if not below. In short he must be recruited and trained. The potluck application system cannot much longer endure. This is especially true in Southeast Asia, where expertise must be learned or acquired through long experience. No Canadian grows up in an atmosphere which allows him even elementary understanding of the Asian national character.
My conclusions in this sphere are these:

column2: Canada has six embassies and five trade commissions in Southeast Asia, in seven of the 15 nations in that region. In other words we are vastly under represented.
There is a great need for specialization in our foreign service, either through training or experience or both.

column1: The Address-^Mr. Sherman

column2: To permit and encourage specialization among foreign service officers the Department of External Affairs should provide incentives to persons who wish to devote themselves to Canada's service in foreign countries of a particular type, or to areas of diplomacy at home.
To provide for recruitment of specialized and expert personnel, the department should undertake an extensive program of public relations and recruitment in universities across Canada.

Canada must divorce itself from the notion that the diplomatic corps is a club. It must prepare itself fully for the kind of knowledge that is needed, and will be needed, in all areas of the world, particularly in Southeast Asia, where more than one half the world's people live.

column1: Having said this, in the time which remains to me I should like to say something about the affairs of Canada at home, the feelings of Canadians and what it is to be a Canadian in this particular year. A House of Commons session of record length has ended and a new one, the second session of the twenty seventh Parliament, is well begun. With the great events of centennial summer now upon us, I feel honoured and privileged to take part in the work of this legislative chamber and to participate in this debate.

I am sure all members of this house, like myself, and all Canadians, will be feeling much satisfaction this spring and summer in their nationality and in their country. This is a great year in which to be a Canadian. With Expo '67, the armed forces tattoo, the panAmerican games, the confederation train, the confederation caravans, the centennial canoe race and all the other pageants great and small which are being presented so successfully in honour of our 100th birthday, we are winning international recognition this summer as one of the most dynamic and exciting countries in the world.

I remember that when I was a schoolboy, far-away fields looked enticingly green. Today for young men and women of high school and university age there is no field so green and so full of promise as Canada. There is a feeling in our country today which was not present a quarter of a century ago. It is a feeling of new ground being broken, new horizons glimpsed, new opportunity at home and a new, assured Canadian personality emerging. It is my opinion that this new Canadian promise reflects itself clearly in our national politics, and if those politics appear
tumultuous at times, it is because we are living a tumultuous chapter in Canadian history.

We have much to celebrate as Canadians in our centennial year. In the shadow of the most powerful and possibly the most persuasive nation the world has ever known we have clung to our Canadian identity, tended it, nurtured it and we are bringing it to bloom.

In the explosive climate generated by two founding races which have not always been charitable toward each other we have so far followed the voice and the path of the moderate man and avoided the temptation to anger. In an almost impossible geographical setting which would have dismayed many a less tenacious people we have scattered a comparative handful of men and women over a rugged, northern land mass of nearly four million square miles, covering half a continent, and we have held it together. We have built two transcontinental railroads, two transcontinental and international air lines, two transcontinental television and broadcasting networks, a transcontinental super highway, one of the world's greatest inland waterway systems and a coast to coast network of international airports that rank with any on the face of the earth.

We have built two of the world's greatest cities, and 20 others that are smaller but all of which are bursting with growth. We have built or are building 50 universities. We have plumbed the depths of our soil for petroleum and precious minerals; we have sown our vast prairies with wheat and fed half the world with the harvests. We have led the world in making many advances in the fields of medicine and science.

We have begun at last to address ourselves seriously to the arts, and there are hopeful signs that we are about to address ourselves seriously to scientific and industrial research. We have introduced social and humanitarian legislation which has brought security and freedom from worry to millions of our countrymen who without such measures would carry crushing burdens of financial care. Through depression we have persevered; out of trouble we have triumphed.

There is nothing we cannot make of Canada, you and I. As a country she is limited only by our human limitations. The glories and the triumphs of her first century in confederation may be as nothing in comparison with the triumphs of her second century yet to come. But there are areas of human labour and endeavour to which we must yet
turn our attention, especially in the field of human relations. I have mentioned some of the tremendous physical tasks which have been achieved. Among those still remaining to be done are these:

It will be our task to solve the problem of urban sprawl with all its related crises. It will be our task to open up our north country, to harness our huge reserves of fresh water, to tap new reserves of mineral wealth and to eliminate as far as possible the differences and discrepancies in regional growth and development across the country. It will be our task to build new roads and new towns, new sattelite cities and industrial cities. We may have to subsidize people to encourage them to settle in the north and push back the Arctic frontier. It will be our task to solve the problem of air pollution, and to solve the problems of old age. We shall have to find a cure for cancer. There are a thousand challenges of this nature, many of them yet unimagined.

But these are physical assignments or challenges. And important as they are, I believe them less important than some of the challenges which face our country in the field of human relations. The field of human relations, in my opinion, is the indispensable ground in which the foundations of Canada's second century must be dug. We must search that field for solid ground. If we sink our shafts in dry, sterile soil, if we dig in the barren sands of the status quo, if we try to rest our supports on the swamp of special interest groups, our structure will fail and the second Canadian century will crumble. But if we search that field earnestly and conscientiously for the good earth of human dignity, and if we build there, then the dreams we have for Canada will last not just into a second century but for a thousand years.

For I believe, and I think most Canadians would agree with me, that it is just as important to find a cure for war as to find a cure for cancer. It is just as important to rid our hearts of prejudice as to rid our air of pollution. It is just as important to redevelop our Indians as to redevelop our downtown areas. It is just as important to strengthen the fabric of Canadian life as to strengthen our reserves. And it is infinitely more important to the future of this country that we build highways of understanding between English and French and all ethnic and racial groups than that we build highways of concrete into the Arctic. This really is the challenge which faces us in this house, as well as all Canadians outside, as we enter our second century.
DEBATES
The Address-Mr. Gregoire

Some three decades ago Franklin Roosevelt coined a phrase that became a challenge and a battle cry for a whole generation of his countrymen. He told them ""This generation of Americans has a rendezvous with destiny."" They responded to the call. Now, it seems tc me, sir, those words ring with far more significance for Canada than they ever did for the United States in Franklin Roosevelt's time.

One of the pre-eminent emotions in Canada today is social tension, tension between the whole of the country and its parts, tension among many of the parts themselves, tension so critical on some levels that possibly the very concept of Canada has been threatened. I believe this generation of Canadians has a rendezvous with destiny. As no other generation of Canadians before us, we and our children have the responsibility for deciding and determining whether there is going to be a Canada at all in the future, and what kind and type of Canada it is going to be. This is the substance of the Canadian experiment, and it is we who may determine whether that experiment finally succeeds or fails. In this context and in that connection, sir, I take this opportunity to wish all of us in this house, all of us in Canada, good luck in our careers as citizens and builders of this great country.

,Progressive Conservative,,Louis Ralph (Bud) Sherman,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6a20bcf5-076c-47f5-af31-032a26ad6da0&Language=E&Section=ALL
2490538,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.18.1.4,1967-05-19,acd5380d-f564-427d-821a-4528ecdba8f3,ca.m.9577,Mr. Gilles Gregoire (Lapointe):,,SPEECH FROM THE THRONE,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I should not like to be too long, and I will only make a few observations.
The motion for voting an address presented by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) and seconded by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cote) reads as follows:
We, Her Majesty's most loyal and dutiful subjects, the House of Commons of Canada-

Most loyal and dutiful subjects. Mr. Speaker, I will simply say that I am opposed to the motion, because I do not consider myself as a subject but rather as a free citizen. In my opinion, the motion should not be written in those terms.

How can we, in 1967, in the middle of the twentieth century and in Canada, a country which calls itself free, begin by the formula ""We, Her Majesty's most loyal and dutiful subjects"" when, on the contrary, we are elected by Canadian citizens in our respective ridings; how could we renounce our allegiance
The Address-Mr. Gregoire to our electorate and recognize another authority than which delegated us here?

Mr. Speaker, one may smile at that, but nevertheless the idea is embodied in all aspects of Canadian life over the past 100 years. Those who were present at the opening of Expo remember several details of the ceremony of which we cannot be proud. For example, the official band played three times ""God Save the Queen"", the national anthem of England. Three times. And that, before playing ""O Canada"" even once. Three times, the national anthem of a foreign country. And those who were there, among Canadian citizens, and who were official delegates, diplomats from Africa, South America, Asia, Japan, Belgium, England, France, Germany, Italy, the United States-from 70 different countries-were surprised to find that the national anthem played here in Canada was ""God Save the Queen"", and that happened three times.

I also recall that, in 1965, the International Parliamentary Union held its meeting here in Ottawa. At that time, the representatives from 70 countries, members of parliament and senators, were meeting here to discuss problems relating to parliamentary government throughout the world. And there was a concert in the Capitol theatre, here in Ottawa, played by the symphonic orchestra of Toronto. It was a very beautiful concert and it was very successful. The symphony, directed by a Japanese, was excellent. There were two great Canadian stars, Richard Verreault and another one, a soprano, whose name I cannot recall.

2490540,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.18.1.6,1967-05-19,acd5380d-f564-427d-821a-4528ecdba8f3,ca.m.9577,Mr. Gregoire:,,SPEECH FROM THE THRONE,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,No, not Maureen Forrester who is also very well known. That was two years ago, and I have forgotten the name. At the beginning of the concert, what did one hear? Everybody got up for the national anthem, but ""God Save the Queen"", was what they heard. All the representatives, members of Parliament, senators from about 75 countries throughout the world were looking at each other and wondering if they were not in an English colony, in the seventeenth, eighteenth or nineteenth century.

As a Canadian citizen, I felt embarrassed at this point, in front of all those guests from all countries who were invited here in Ottawa, in Canada. And what was played for them: ""God Save the Queen,"" the national anthem of England.
Mr. Speaker, about two days ago, last weekend, I was visiting a foreign pavilion at the Expo, when a foreign representative, I do not remember from what country, came and asked me:
column2: Tell me, are your Canadian dollars

column1: guaranteed by England? Is it England that guarantees your dollars? I said: No. And then I asked him: What made you say that? He showed me a dollar bill and said: The picture of the Queen of England is on your bills. Are they guaranteed by England and is that why you have to put the picture of a foreign queen on your currency? I said: No, it is a leftover from the colonialism of the last century or two.

And here we claim to be Canadian citizens. We would like to make the citizens of Quebec, Ontario, etc. believe that they are Canadian citizens, whereas everything in our life is permeated by colonialism, without end or logic, right in 1967 and when, throughout the world, the countries with the least pride and dignity have broken off those colonial ties. Here in Canada we keep them. Our national anthem is still ""God Save the Queen"", as evidenced by the fact that it is played first. If, at least, it were played second; no, it is played first and three times in a row, before ""O Canada"". And those who were there will recall how it was played in a macabre, funerary and funereal rhythm, in a way I have never heard it played before. Those in attendance remember very well, and can testify to that. And it was played last, as if with fear. England's national anthem first. On our money, the picture of the Queen of England. And it is always the same. We are hosts to foreign countries but we have nothing to show except symbols, choirs, national hymns and great themes of another country as if we were a colony. If it were only a symbol, Mr. Speaker, but we are too penetrated by that colonial style, not only in the political field but also in the economic field, by that feeling of dependence, as if we could not have, at home, sufficient dignity and pride to give ourselves a free country where we would no longer be considered as subjects but as free citizens.

Mr. Speaker, we have not achieved this Canadian pride. It is not surprising then that in Quebec, I, at least, and many others, are trying to give ourselves a homeland because one has not been secured for us elsewhere. We will do all that needs to be done to have a homeland instead of living as colonials.
Some people may like it. I see the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) who still is a
Quebec citizen, a Canadian. Does he approve?
I would like to have his views. Does he approve of the playing of the national hymn of another country first, at international ceremonies in Canada? Is the Postmaster General proud of that?

2490590,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.18.1.56,1967-05-19,59a069df-b395-42e0-8bbe-1cd082c90611,ca.m.1232,Mr. Ralph Cowan (York-Humber):,,SPEECH FROM THE THRONE,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,Mr. Speaker, I am taking the opportunity of participating in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne in order to deal with two subjects in particular which could occupy the whole of the time allotted to a private member. I do so because in my mind and in the opinion of other hon. members of the house these two important matters have been brushed aside by the cabinet, in outlining the work of parliament and accomplishing the desires of the people, for other purposes which are not as vital.
I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the order paper of the house. On page 19 of today's order paper for Friday, May 19 you will find a resolution standing in my name which reads as follows:

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the expediency of introducing legislation for the creation of a criminal injuries compensation board to hear the pleas of persons who have suffered permanent injury or disability as the victims of crime and award compensation to such persons or their dependants as would seem fair in the circumstances, and wherever possible to do so, to impose payment of compensation by criminals to those they have injured.

I first placed that resolution on the order paper in January, 1966. As everyone knows, under the rules of the house it was nothing but a private member's resolution. Being a private member's resolution and having been on the order paper since January, 1966, the first and only opportunity ever provided by the house leader to discuss the matter was on Wednesday, June 8, 1966. One hour was allotted to the discussion of the resolution. It was talked out by one of the exalted members of the party, a parliamentary secretary, and it
died a natural death never to reappear again on the order paper. I was forced, therefore, to reintroduce it in this month of May in the new session of parliament.
The other day the hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Choquette) rose in the house and asked this question:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the hon. Minister of Justice and Attorney General. Since a number of honest citizens think that our society makes many efforts to improve the lot of criminals, I should like to ask the minister the following question.
Is he giving consideration to setting up or interesting the provinces in setting up a program of compensation for crime victims or the families of crime victims?
The Minister of Justice and Attorney General (Mr. Trudeau) replied as follows:

Mr. Speaker, this question has also been raised by certain correspondents. I am studying the problem at the present time. As the hon. member is aware, there is also here a question of constitutional law, for such compensation could come from the provinces instead of the central government. However, in that case, negotiations could be undertaken with the provinces.

It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that when you do not intend to do anything in the parliament of Canada you simply stand up and say there is a constitutional question involved relating to the provinces. This is supposed to be the end of it for the rest of time. Here we have an answer on May 11 by the Minister of Justice, a man in whom I have the greatest confidence, which suggests there is a question of constitutional law involved. Let us take the Truscott case. I do not want to discuss it at this time because feelings are easily aroused. However, I will take the Truscott case as an illustration because it is before us at the present time.

Here is a man who has been convicted of murder and is undergoing a life sentence in Kingston penitentiary at Collins Bay or Portsmouth, wherever he may be. In any event, he is down in the Kingston area undergoing a life sentence because that was the sentence of the court. Who is paying the cost of giving him three meals a day, maintaining him in warm surroundings, giving him a bed at night, providing the necessary chaplaincy services, looking after his recreation and seeing that he does not become too obese or does not lose weight through lack of eating? The parliament of Canada is providing the wherewithal to keep criminals in luxury while the bodies of their victims lie in their graves.

When people like the hon. member for Lotbiniere ask the cabinet if any consideration is being given to paying compensation to the victims of criminal acts, they are given the answer quite quickly that there is here a question of constitutional law. The government keeps right on feeding Truscott and making certain he does not miss a meal, all at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers. When they are asked, is there any compensation for the victims of these crimes, back comes the high-sounding answer that there is a question of constitutional law involved and the rights of the provinces must be maintained. If we can afford to pay the cost of keeping the criminal, surely we can afford to offer some compensation to the victims of crime when the victims are absolutely innocent of any complicity in the matter.

When this subject was discussed on June 8, 1966, almost a year ago, a large number of hon. members supported the principle of this resolution. One of the ablest members in the house, the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Forest), in supporting the principle stated he felt that since compensation for injury was concerned it might be a provincial matter. I respect the hon. member's legal knowledge and I respect his judgment. Possibly there is an element of provincial jurisdiction involved. However, as long as this house is willing to pay for the upkeep of criminals out of federal funds I believe we should pay for the compensation of the victim of criminal acts on exactly the same ground.

I should like to refer to a murder case to which I have made frequent reference in this house involving a seven year old girl in my own church congregation in Toronto. The man who was accused of the murder of this little child entered a defence of insanity. His lawyer won the argument in that case and the moment he did so this man was immediately incarcerated in the asylum for the criminally insane maintained by the Ontario government at Penetanguishene, about eight miles from a summer home I have maintained since 1937. This institution is well known to me and it renders a magnificent service.

It does seem odd to me as a Canadian taxpayer, and I have been a taxpayer for a long number of years, that when a chap like Truscott is convicted of murdering a little girl he serves his life sentence in Kingston penitentiary and Ottawa looks after providing three meals, a warm bed and warm accommodation, but when this other man is accused of murdering a little seven year old girl from the congregation of Victoria Presbyterian

The Address-Mr. Cowan Church and is judged insane he goes to an asylum and becomes the responsibility of the taxpayers of the province of Ontario. In my opinion, this is splitting hairs beyond reason.

If you are going to argue that compensation for the victims of crime is a matter of provincial jursidiction and if you are going to have the Canadian taxpayer shoulder the cost of looking after the criminals, then the Canadian taxpayer will certainly jump at the opportunity of offering compensation to the victims of crime. If the government will bring forward legislation I have no doubt parliament will pass it in a day. I might point out that my interest in this matter has extended over a number of years because as a newspaper reporter many years ago I covered more than one murder trial. As I pointed out in the debate on capital punishment, I was the foreman of a jury when I was 19. This is illegal because one should be 21 but the judge appointed me because, as I emphasized when speaking, I was the only man in the room where the murder trial was being held who could write English. I just refer to that because I was working on a murder case when I was only 19 years of age. This goes back quite a few years and I covered a number of murder cases for newspapers over the years.

I have come face to face with the victims of crimes and in police court work I have also come across the victims of crimes such as merciless beatings, hit and run drivers, and cases where gas was turned on in a room while a person slept and he was a physical wreck thereafter because of the effect on his lungs. There are many victims of crime other than the victims of murder. I suggest that parliament should provide compensation to the victims of criminal acts, no matter what the nature of the act may be.

As I mentioned, the resolution I introduced was discussed for one hour on June 8, 1966 when it was talked out. At that time a member of the house made this statement, and I quote from page 6168 of Hansard for June 8, 1966:
-I am doubtful about what the resolution means.

I do not think that we should hold up such legislation until the hon. member for Anti-gonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) is able to comprehend the significance of the motion, because the people of Canada want legislation for the compensation of victims and they want it fast.
It is interesting to note that three provinces in Canada have begun to take some action

The Address-Mr. Cowan with regard to introducing measures for the compensation of victims. I have a newspaper clipping of December 9 of last year from the Winnipeg Free Press indicating that the Manitoba government is making a bid to aid crime victims. I also have a clipping taken from the Toronto Globe and Mail for February 11 of this year which points out that the Saskatchewan government is bringing in a law to aid the victims of crime. I also read in the Vancouver Sun for February 28, 1967 that British Columbia crime casualties are to get aid. So there are three provinces in Canada that have taken steps to compensate victims of criminal acts, and I see signs that the province of Quebec is going to take similar action.

One might ask, since the provinces are moving why not let this matter go ahead? I maintain that we should have uniform legislation on this subject right across Canada, and since the federal government is paying for the upkeep of convicted criminals I think it should also pay compensation to victims of crime.

I would not criticize a single one of the bills that are now being brought forward by provinces because I am anxious to see them become law in the provinces concerned. I am also anxious to see one law for the whole of Canada but I will help these provinces in any way possible to get this legislation on their statute books. I have long believed that half a loaf is better than none.

It is quite interesting to compare terms of the three bills in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia to which I have referred. As I mentioned earlier, there are signs that Quebec will take some action, though I have no details as to what action Quebec is considering other than that I know there are men and women in the province of Quebec who believe that victims of crime should be compensated.

Let me outline some of the disparities in the legislation of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia. I point out that according to the Saskatchewan bill, which I think is the best of the three, the victim will not be required to pursue legal action before applying for compensation to the compensation board. That determination has been made by those in Saskatchewan who framed the legislation.
When one turns to the legislation that is suggested for Manitoba one sees it is necessary under that bill for a victim there to have exhausted legal action before he can apply

for compensation. The Manitoba white paper on this subject states that it is proposed that the victim, before being eligible to receive compensation, must exhaust all legal remedies and all other forms of public assistance. That language is in almost direct opposition to that used in the Saskatchewan legislation. But I say to the members of this house through you, Mr. Speaker, that I sincerely hope both provinces put this legislation on their statute books because they will at least have started something which I hope the federal government will take up and bring to national fruition by passing a uniform act.

It is interesting to note that in British Columbia Attorney General Bonner told the British Columbia legislature that the responsibility for compensation will be placed squarely on the shoulders of the municipalities involved.

2490598,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.18.1.64,1967-05-19,59a069df-b395-42e0-8bbe-1cd082c90611,ca.m.1232,Mr. Cowan:,,SPEECH FROM THE THRONE,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,Mr. Speaker, to answer the question I would say that no one could compensate me for the loss of my child, but I simply say that in Great Britain that sort of thing is being done. Last July that lead was followed also by the state of New York.

There is a growing realization that society owes protection to its individuals, and where society fails to give that protection it should take a hand in giving compensation to the victims of crimes. To take an example, it
May 19, 19S7

The Address-Mr. Cowan should provide for the widow and children of the murdered breadwinner. Of course, there are many other instances where innocents suffer because of violent crimes of which some member of their family has been a victim.

The resolution to which I referred asks for the appointment of a criminal compensation board to adjudicate on all applications that may come forward. Precedents in New Zealand, Great Britain, California and New York state are building up all the time, and I understand that Saskatchewan-God bless her-will have her law in effect by July or August of this year. I maintain that the federal cabinet should be taking a hand in this matter and should be doing so fast, particularly since parliament voted 143 to 112 to maintain capital punishment and we are advised that a second effort is to be made to abolish it. But there is no mention of the victims of crime in the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker.
I hope I have made myself clear. I believe I am stating the opinions of many members of the House of Commons who have spoken to me over the years on this important matter.

I should like to move on to the question of citizenship. Over the past several years I have referred more than once to an Italian-Canadian family. I dislike using the words ""Italian-Canadian"" because I do not like hyphenated descriptions of Canadians. To me we are all Canadians. I call these people Italian-Canadians because they were born in Italy and are naturalized Canadian citizens who have returned to their homeland and are living in Italy again.
In four consecutive speeches from the throne, those of May 16, 1963; February 18, 1964; April 5, 1965; and January 18, 1966, we have had beautiful clauses reading for example, this way:
-a change in the Canadian Citizenship Act will be proposed to ensure full equality of rights for all Canadian citizens wherever they were born.
Or reading:
My government will propose legislation to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act, in order to ensure equality of rights for all citizens.
And here is another one:
A measure will be placed before you to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act, particularly in order to ensure full equality of rights for all Canadian citizens wherever they were born.
We have had four promises and no action. I have in my hands the speech from the throne delivered on Monday, May 8, not two weeks

ago. It runs to pages and pages of fine type. 1 have read it in full at least twice and partially two or three times, and not once in that speech from the throne, which is not yet two weeks old, is there a single, solitary reference to the Canadian Citizenship Act. We have been told in four speeches from the throne, that amendments to the act would be introduced. We are told that the amendments are ready, that they have been prepared and that the regulations also are drawn up.

The situation against which I protest is that a naturalized Canadian citizen who leaves the country for a period of years must have his passport validated at the nearest Canadian embassy every three years or it will expire. In the instance of this Italian family who lived in Weston in the riding of York-Humber, they had their passports validated at the end of the third year of their stay in Italy and at the end of their sixth year in Italy.

The Canadian and United States dollars go much farther in Italy than in Canada or the United States and many naturalized Canadians return to their homelands in their years of retirement because of the increased purchasing power their money has there. A brother of a cabinet minister spends several months of the year in Spain for that reason, and no one thinks any the worse of him. He is stretching his Canadian dollar as far as it will go.

Here I am talking of an Italian-Canadian family who have lived in Italy for over nine years. Because there was illness in the family at the end of the third three year period when their passports had to be validated they did not do so. When they decided to come back to York-Humber to visit daughters and sons they have in the riding the Canadian embassy told them that their passports had expired because they had not been validated within three years. This elderly couple was really upset about the matter. And why not? They have foresworn allegiance to Italy and have sworn allegiance to the Queen of Canada, the Queen of this country. But this country said: ""We do not want you any more; you did not get your passport validated within three years at the nearest Canadian embassy.""

I am a natural born Canadian. I do not have to get my passport validated at any time, should I be outside the country, because I can come back to Canada, my birthplace. I have not foresworn allegiance to it. But if a naturalized Canadian citizen living outside
the country does not have his passport validated every three years he loses his citizenship.

I took the matter up with hon. Mr. Favreau who at that time was minister of immigration. I say with great pleasure, and I would be pleased to say it louder, that he straightened the whole matter out in one hour. He agreed that the Canadian Citizenship Act should be amended and that naturalized Canadians ought not to be in the position where, if they are outside the country for more than three years, they must get their passports validated or lose their citizenship. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):,Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration,SPEECH FROM THE THRONE,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,Mr. Speaker, I too would like to take this occasion to compliment the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They were excellent speeches. I believe very few of us have heard better oratory than we did on that occasion.

In the few minutes at my disposal I should like to discuss an area about which I do not believe there has been a great deal of discussion during this debate. I refer to the current state of labour legislation, the desires of the labour movement, the effect that the aims and aspirations of the labour movement have had upon the government and, to a degree, the effect that government action has had on the labour movement itself. Also I should like to discuss what this development has been in political terms and how it relates to the Liberal party. I believe, that because of government action in the areas of major concern to labour and because of changing times the Liberal party and this government now have an entree into the labour movement itself which has not been available to this party for many years. The elements which have contributed to this development are the rapidly changing circumstances of our society and the record of the government.

I do not believe that any political party, least of all my own which is a national party in scope and which for so many years has formed the government of this country, can view with any confidence the situation when one observes that the officials of the trade union movement-and I speak in terms of the trade union elite, the top leaders at the national level and the middle echelon of the local unions-are becoming so identified with one particular political party, the New Democratic party. I believe this places a responsibility on the Liberal party to examine this situation and take whatever action is necessary to rectify it, because I believe we can serve ourselves better as a party and serve the Canadian people better if we have contact with the leaders of the labour movement, welcome them into our ranks and see that they have an active and influential voice in the government and in our party structure.

I should like to elaborate on why I feel the record of this government has laid the basis for this type of entry on the part of the Liberal party into the official ranks of labour and why I think we have laid the basis for an appeal to these men of whom I speak. After a very cursory examination of this record I

The Address-Mr. Munro believe it will be seen that those leaders of the labour movement must take a new look at the Liberal party as a vehicle and as an adequate political party for them to be associated with in order to realize their aims and aspirations.

In looking at this situation further I believe there are three general large domestic areas of prime concern to labour. The first would have to be social welfare proposals and programs. The second would be labour legislation and the need for reform in this area, and in the narrow sense I would specify labour legislation. The third would have to be manpower policies designed to cope with technological change and over-all economic policies, e (3:40 p.m.)

What then has been our record in these three prime areas of domestic concern to labour? Certainly under the first general heading, social welfare policy, since 1963 there have been massive legislative programs implemented which have re-oriented the whole basis of our social welfare structure in this country. In this regard let me mention the Old Age Security Act amendments which increased old age pensions to a universal $75 as a base and tied them into the cost of living. There was further legislation lowering the age level a year at a time so that by 1970 citizens 65 years of age will receive the basic old age pension. Let me also mention the Canada Pension Plan which I think ranks as one of the finest contributory pension plans in the free world. It has provided the means for universal coverage for all Canadians in our work force. The benefits payable under this plan when coupled with old age security give as generous an over-all benefit to Canadians upon retirement as those enjoyed anywhere in the free world.

The Canada Assistance Plan embodied a government endeavour to rationalize our multitudinous provincial and federal welfare schemes so they all could tie into a universal test, namely, the needs test, thus doing away with the arbitrary limits under the categorical programs where the $75 is the limit irrespective of the need of a recipient. The Canada Assistance Plan does away with that obstacle, and I think it will lay the basis for a dovetailing of all our welfare programs. It gives special benefit to all those needy people who are too young to receive old age security but who, because of some disability, are not and cannot fall within the coverage of the Canada Pension Plan, and it does not limit them to the $75 which is woefully inadequate.
The Address-Mr. Munro

Next let me point out the introduction of medicare which was a prime political rallying cry in this country not so many years ago. This has now been implemented by legislation and will be in force next year, the federal government being obligated to undertake 50 per cent of the cost.

I point out lastly the guaranteed income supplement which provides a further sum of money to those of our older citizens who are receiving the old age pension. This is based on an income test which obviates the necessity for the humiliating investigations that always accompanied the means test. It provides $30 per month for those who qualify under the income test, bringing their income up to $105 per month.

Certainly it would have to be conceded that in this first area of over-all concern in the domestic policy field, the record is quite impressive. It would be conceded immediately that it is not perfect and that there are other areas left to be dealt with including the cost of drugs and their inclusion in the future under the medicare plan. It would also include a widening of the coverage under medicare to cover dental care and so on. However, the basis for this has been laid which will guarantee that no Canadian will lack the fundamental means with which to survive, with shelter, food and the other necessities of life.

I say the basis has been laid and further programs will be of a minor nature not involving any fundamental ideals or ideology. They will just round out the basic policies that have been adopted. I have referred to drugs being included under medicare. Perhaps another over-all new policy which we must talk about now as a political party, and I am sure this is being discussed more by members of this party than those of any other, is the guaranteed annual income for all. This will be under intensive discussion by all politicians and certainly all economists in this country during the next few years. It is a policy which I am sure will inevitably be implemented in this country, and perhaps the sooner the better. If it should come, and I hope it does, it will involve the dismantling of perhaps all our welfare policies and the guaranteeing of an over-all minimum income for everyone. This seems to be endorsed by outstanding economists in the United States, some of whose sympathies are with the left and some with the right in the political spectrum. There seems to be a consensus developing that this is a wise policy.

I have referred to some of the policies in this prime area which we have implemented as a party along with one over-all new policy, the guaranteed income which is under intensive study. I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for the suggestion in a recent speech that a task force be set up to study the implications of a guaranteed income for all Canadians.

The second area of prime concern to labour would be the labour legislation itself. We can look at our record in this regard with considerable pride. We can look at the Canada Labour (Standards) Code which sets minimum hours of work, minimum hours of overtime and minimum wage laws. We can look at our Canada Labour Safety Code which brought in a comprehensive safety formula to be adhered to for the protection of employees while they are on the job.

Another item which we implemented as one of our commitments is collective bargaining rights for civil servants. Our major commitments have been kept and our record here is a source of pride to many Liberals. Certainly it is a motivation to labour to look hard at Liberal party programs when they are advocated. This record is certainly justification for the sincere belief on the part of labour that these new programs will be implemented.

In terms of new policies in this over-all area we are also moving forward. I refer hon. members to the discussion going on in respect of compulsory arbitration and the discussion going on throughout the country regarding the use of injunctions. The position of this party in this area was laid out very well at the policy conference of the Liberal party held last October. The position taken at that time was spelled out in the following terms:
Therefore this convention urges that the task force consider immediately:

It can be accepted that many members of this party wholeheartedly endorse those proposals which embody, in general terms, our attitude in respect of contentious areas such as compulsory arbitration and injunctions. I believe there is considerable sympathy within our party that compulsory arbitration should not be resorted to under any circumstances nor regarded as an instrument in solving labour disputes. I also believe that injunctions have proved inadequate as a means of resolving the differences between labour and management and have had the reverse effect of exacerbating the situation, creating further hard feeling between labour and management and making a meeting of minds all the more difficult. I believe a great deal of reform could be implemented in this respect and that we should undertake an extensive reform of our legislation in this area.

In this context I would quote the position taken at a recent C.L.C. convention in a paper presented by Mr. Osier which I believe was backed forcibly by many political spokesmen and many people in the ranks of labour and management. The position there taken-and I think it is a reasonable one-was not that all injunctions should be banned, because Mr. Osier did not think there was a possibility that any parliament would take such action, but that the following recommendations should be adopted:
No injunction may be granted by any court in
connection with a labour dispute except after a hearing of testimony of witnesses in open court, on notice to those it is proposed to enjoin, with an opportunity to adduce their own evidence.
Another proposal in this area is as follows:

No injunction may be granted by any court in connection with a labour dispute, except after specific findings of every fact that is legally required to support such injunction and any such injunction may only prohibit

column2: specific acts requested in the notice of motion for such injunction and
the commission of such acts by particular persons or organizations named in the injunction.

column1: This was another proposal:

That is very similar to the law in the United States, the Norris-LaGuardia act which I think has proven its effectiveness. I 27053-29

The Address-Mr. Munro believe we should copy that act in this country except that we should go further and say that jurisdiction in respect of injunctions in the labour-management context should be handled by labour relations boards as distinct from the courts. The personnel of the labour relations boards are composed of experienced people from management and labour who are better equipped to deal more realistically with this type of remedy.

In the area of injunctions I think the research that is now going on will afford some basis for alternative solutions. I believe that the recommendations to which I have referred are worthy of implementation by the government. In the area of compulsory arbitration I have indicated that I do not believe this system has been effective. I think we must reject it as a means of settling labour disputes. In those situations where there is absolutely no alternative, where there is a national emergency, where consultation and negotiation have not been effective in resolving the differences, and where massive unemployment may affect the whole nation despite all the efforts of both sides and the intervention of government mediation services, in short where no solution can be found, then compulsory arbitration should be imposed only by parliament. These are two prime areas of contention with regard to which I think this party is prepared to take a position. I do not think that all political parties would take a firm, unalterable position in these areas until the Dean Woods inquiry has been completed, which inquiry is looking into all these questions. I believe the results of this inquiry will afford a basis from which we can realistically assess what are the best methods to be used to resolve labour-management disputes in this country.

There is one other area of very grave concern to the labour movement and all citizens of Canada. It is a matter of grave concern to the Canadian government and, I believe, all political parties. I refer to the principle enunciated by Mr. Justice Freedman. I do not think there has been as much discussion as there might have been on this principle. I believe it is a good principle and should be endorsed. I would quote in essence Mr. Justice Freedman's recommendations. I think the house will agree that they are quite reasonable. In essence, Mr. Justice Freedman's principal recommendations are as follows:
Notice of intent, accompanied by adequate details of the company's proposals;
The Address-Mr. Munro
That is what the company must give to the union. The notice must indicate to the union just what the company intends to do in terms of technological change. The second proposal in:
Arbitration to assess the effect of the company's plan upon the working conditions of the employes with a view to determining whether such effect would be material or otherwise;

Of course, that is what takes place during the currency of a collective agreement. The third recommendation is that there should be negotiations at the terminal date of the collective agreement. It is difficult for me to comprehend any other more reasonable solution to these problems. There has been a great deal of discussion in this respect; seminars have been held by management and labour. I do not think that anyone has yet come up with a more adequate solution. I believe that these findings of Mr. Justice Freedman warrant adoption as a matter of government policy.

That, Mr. Speaker, is a short review of what we have done in the more or less narrow field of labour relations. I have dealt with some of the major items of concern to labour about which this government is concerned.

The third area of major domestic concern in the field of labour is connected with manpower policies. Here I think the record of the government and this party deserves considerable commendation. I believe it is a record that the labour movement of this country must acknowledge as deserving of their accolades. I refer to the implementation of the labour mobility program and the occupational training program. These two programs should have far reaching effects. Under the labour mobility program we give grants to workers to move from an area of low employment to one with more adequate employment opportunities. We make allowances to the worker to set up a home in another area. We make it, in other words, easy for him to move. He is not penalized because of the move but is subsidized to do so in order to obtain gainful employment.

The occupational training program is a far reaching one designed to deal with dislocations as a result of technological change. We realize that people dislocated from employment must receive training and in our new society we must constantly be ready to receive new training. We recognize that the current skills of our workers may be obsolete five or ten years from now. This program is

designed to assist workers who suffer dislocation as a result of automation which is introduced into the plants in which they work with the effect that they are no longer required. It gives them an opportunity to take training and obtain the new skills that are required. It also provides them with an income while they are learning new skills.

We still have the technical and vocational training program which is designed to assist our young people, although we are turning this program over to the provinces, as hon. members know, and are gradually phasing out of it. But the basis has been established which provides educational facilities to accomplish our aim. There have been massive federal government contributions in this area for many years. I believe this program is now sufficiently well established for it to be turned over to the provinces.

Another area in which the federal government has taken action in the over-all manpower field is in the setting up of pilot projects in co-operation with the provinces to research new methods of training that will best take into account a person's capabilities and basic education and will provide methods by which his education and skills can be upgraded. This is going to be of great assistance to both management and labour in tackling technological change.

If management decides it is going to have to adopt technological innovations or automation which is going to cause severe dislocation, this service is prepared to give grants to management and labour to assist them in researching this program so the dislocation can be minimized, and at the same time advise on measures for retraining workers presently employed by the plant so they can be effective when the changes are implemented.
