2490626,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.18.1.92,1967-05-19,fec67695-f109-4531-9eda-a768eeaf64d9,ca.m.4469,Mr. Robert Stanbury (York-Scarborough):,,SPEECH FROM THE THRONE,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,Mr. Speaker, as one who had the privilege and the somewhat unnerving experience of making his maiden speech on his first day in this Centennial Parliament, sharing the honour with the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer), I pay the highest tribute to those who followed us in opening the throne speech debate in this second session. No one could have carried out this duty with greater distinction than did the hon. members for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) and Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cote).

Each of us is tempted at such an historic time in our country's life to look back on its accomplishments and those who wrought them. I am grateful to those who, through the century and even before, made their contributions to the building of this nation. We can learn from their labours and I hope we will, but we must not become preoccupied with the past. I suspect the fathers of confederation were more concerned about the future.
I feel the speech from the throne caught that spirit. It looked ahead, setting our sights appropriately high as we enter our second

The Address-Mr. Stanbury century of confederation. I welcome particularly the emphasis on elevating the quality of life and enhancing the environment of our people; the determination to tackle problems which know no jurisdictional boundaries; the federal initiatives promised where provincial action needs to be stimulated and supplemented in the national interest. I should like to talk today about many of the matters forecast for this session. I have decided, however, to talk of none of them. Rather I should like to suggest adding something of value to that impressive program.

Canada's future must be our prime concern today. More than ever it demands that we look outward at the international environment in which our country lives and must live. At this moment in our history when we feel most Canadian, we must recognize more clearly than ever before that we are citizens of the world.

In facing this reality, one paramount challenge looms above all. On it turns to a frightening degree the prospects for eradication of war, of hunger, of illiteracy, or for global destruction in slow or sudden fashion. That challenge is China.
In the May 20, 1967 issue of the New Republic, Harrison E. Salisbury of the New York Times said:
The critical question of our day-indeed the question on which the fate of the United States and the world may soon hinge-is whether America and China are to engage in a land war in Asia.

Mr. Salisbury went on to note that this is a question which has hardly begun to engage the attention of this nation. 2490627,ca.proc.d.1967-05-19.18.1.93,1967-05-19,451d41d6-6f60-40ef-87f1-bd1aea75e8c2,ca.m.1579,Mr. Arnold Peters (Timiskaming):,,SPEECH FROM THE THRONE,CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY,,Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to many of the speeches made in this throne speech debate. I have heard some very interesting and controversial subjects raised, some of which have been supported and others

The Address-Mr. Peters ridiculed. I was particularly interested in a speech made recently by my close neighbour in this chamber, the hon. member for Vil-leneuve (Mr. Caouette), in which he referred to an election to be held in the province of Quebec in a city very close to our capital. The hon. member indicated that much of the news coverage in respect of that election favoured the candidate of the New Democratic party. I think it is time that many of the members who criticize the C.B.C. realized that most news agencies, and I think the C.B.C. is no different from others, as a rule cover news when it is made. If that news is controversial, it is more easily accepted as news. I think the interest being paid to this election probably stems from what is being said in parts of Quebec rather than from a change in the attitude of the C.B.C.

I was particularly surprised at the suggestion that communists were infiltrating the C.B.C. Not long ago I heard that separatists were infiltrating the C.B.C., and I often wonder whether they are the same people. It depends on the horse they are riding at the time and what are their interests. However, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is time some hon. members took a serious look at what is news and what is propaganda in the speeches they are making, and if they are making statements that are worth while, and controversial if necessary, their remarks will find a place in the news.

The hon. member for Villeneuve has had almost a lifetime in this field and should know perhaps better than anyone not to single the socialists out for special attention. When the word ""socialist"" is used we often wonder to whom the hon. member is referring. Some people say there are socialists in the Conservative party, others say there are many socialists in the Liberal party, and some say there are socialists in the New Democratic party. I think that the term as it is now used refers to progressive thought rather than what was meant originally in the philosophical jargon of socialists.

I should like to deal with a problem that was first raised in the throne speech and has since been raised several times. I refer to what parliament is going to do and whether we will be able to develop a new look. I have always been amused by those who say that we can change the rules and make parliament work more effectively.
I have been a member of, and actively participate in, a great many organizations.

Certainly, there was no better school for the manipulation of the rules than the trade union movement. I can remember being in several unions fighting the communist element when they were supposed to be a threat. I am not sure how extensive the threat was, or even if it existed at the time. Certainly, the communists were a very potent force. I can remember that we changed the rules in many ways to take care of that threat.

I can remember when the left wing of the labour movement used to object to the adjournment motion of the meeting. Once everyone who was not too interested in what was going on had left, then they had a majority and would take a vote. They would always win.

The next Sunday there would be another meeting and everybody would be there at the beginning. They would rescind the motion that had been passed at the previous meeting. When supper time came those who were not particularly interested went home, so the motion would be put again and passed. This went on week after week. In order to solve the problem, the rules were changed, but when the rules were changed we found we had given the dissidents, not one opportunity to do this, but that we had created four other opportunities.

It seems to me that the rules of parliament have been developed over a great many years and for specific reasons. If you tamper with them and expect worth-while results, your expectations will not be realized. I think that the problem we have in parliament is not necessarily one of changing or modifying the rules. We need a fairly fundamental change. Let us go back to the throne speech. In any organization, the throne speech would be a sort of timetable for the legislation before the house for this session.

I believe this session should not be like the ones which have passed. Anyone who looked at the order paper at the end of the last session would find as much legislation still on the order paper as we had passed, so we really had not gained any ground at all. There were promises by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that this piece of legislation or that was going to be introduced and passed before the end of the session. Some of my colleagues kept asking for legislation to be introduced. Someone on the other side would say: Yes, we will accept that; that is a very good piece of legislation and should be
passed. We really have not used the throne speech as an agenda, we have not set a pattern of legislation.

I am sure many of the members are not yet aware of the difference between legislation mentioned in the throne speech and legislation introduced during that particular session. Some of the newspapers unkindly referred to the fact the government had decided to dust off every piece of legislation they had and put it in the throne speech. Certainly, it was a very long document, and if they had thought of anything else they would have added it.

This reminds me of the time the Prime Minister was asked about social legislation. He said, ""Yes, we are going to pass it this session. We are going to pass divorce reform, abortion reform, birth control legislation"", and then he added something which sounded like, ""and anything else the N.D.P. can think of"". It seems to me that over the years legislation has been introduced in this manner. You will have to give credit to some of my colleagues because they have proposed a great deal of the legislation that has been put on the order paper in the last 20 years. I believe that this is worth while. However, I do not believe that we should kid the country that the things mentioned in the throne speech are going to be implemented by legislation.

I do not believe it is any secret that many of us would have liked this to be a very special session of parliament. This is centennial year. We are celebrating our one hundredth birthday. I feel there is an obligation on members of parliament to be in their constituencies for at least part of these celebrations. I am not thinking of the major cities, because this may not be true of Montreal or Toronto.

Montreal will probably say Expo is the biggest thing that has ever hit that city-this is probably true-and is their centennial project. Many of the small communities have been able to erect a new town hall, buy a fire truck or put in a waterworks plant as a result of the efforts of the citizens. I believe these efforts demand a higher attention from the elected representatives, and it would seem to me this would involve many of the members being at home at various times. There will likely never be during this session more than three quarters of the members present. It seems to me if this is a logical supposition, then we should make preparations to do something about it.
There has been some reference by some members to the fact that the throne speech
The Address

Mr. Peters debate should have been reduced in length. I agree that the hon. member who moved the address in reply made a good speech. In many respects, his speech indicated that he may have written it. I am sure it was the kind of speech that could have been televised and would have reflected great credit on all members of parliament. It was a flowery speech and indicated the aspirations of the people, and really was not political in the normal sense of the word. I see no reason, Mr. Speaker, why, after a session of 14 months, we could not have decided to shorten the throne speech debate. We have lost these eight days. We could then have gone right into the budget speech and the handling of estimates. We could have decided how many days we wanted so that we could get out of here before July 1.

When I think of the standing committees, that is a good point to digress. Last year some of the standing committees sat for 12 or 13 months. In my opinion, some of them presented excellent reports. These reports have not been considered because most of them were introduced in the last days of the last session. Certainly, the government has not considered the legislation flowing from these reports. It seems to me members of parliament must be rather stupid if they want to have these estimates referred back to standing committees so they can do the same amount of work over again.

Why should reports be presented to parliament when parliament can give no consideration to these reports? It seems to me this would be a good time to waive the sending of estimates to the standing committees, except for those which are required to be sent according to law. Perhaps even this could be waived. Perhaps we should pay some special attention to some of the joint and special committees which have not reported. I am not saying they have not reported because of delay in the other place. The delay was probably the result of the inability of our members to attend. These committees could be reconstituted by the government and could complete their work. In so far as estimates going to committees are concerned, I do not know whether members want to go through this sort of ritualistic dance, and want to spend their time in committees. The government has had to scratch to get members to gc to committees. Certainly a number of Liberal backbenchers were kept busy, but they could have been busy in other fields this year. It is
The Address-Mr. Peters an obligation on all members of parliament to accept some of the thousands of invitations to important functions in different areas of Canada.

We could have waived the throne speech, Mr. Speaker. Why didn't we? We did not because four or five members got together in the back room and tried to make a deal. This sort of deal never works, because such deals are made in the back room. If we are not prepared to state on the floor of this house that we will waive the debate on the throne speech or the debate on the budget speech, or curtail certain discussion of the estimates for this year for the specific purpose of allowing members to participate in centennial celebrations, then such arrangements will not be made. And I am prepared to see that they are not made.

The throne speech appeared to be the kind of speech that everyone could agree with. There were reminiscences about our history, homage was paid those who have gone before us, reference was made to past achievements, to the problems we face today and to the aspirations that our young people have for tomorrow and the years to come. We could have left it at that.

I am told, Mr. Speaker-I may be wrong, and if I am there will be much disappointment-that the budget will not contain anything sensational. And there is no reason why it should: There will be no election this year. Everybody will be so tired by the end of the year that they will not want to campaign for six or eight weeks, so there will be no election. Indeed, the kind of arrangements that have been made recently indicate that there is no chance of even an accident happening.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that we should let the country know whether or not members of parliament intend to participate in centennial celebrations. If we do not, then let us say so. I want to be in a position where I can honestly tell the people in my riding that they cannot count on me for July or August because I will not be at home. I shall be able to tell them that I have a job to do in Ottawa, and that although I think their celebrations may be much more important, I was elected to represent them here so I shall be unable to attend their celebrations.

If some arrangements are made, Mr. Speaker, then, of course, we shall have to sacrifice something. I should like to be able to talk about 20 subjects on this throne speech, or on the budget speech, but I can pass them up. I have done so before. Nothing is new. We
can use our legislation over and over again until we can make a change, so we should be able to give some things up.

In return for this the government should be willing to give something up. It seems to me that one of the things they will have to give up is the idea that they have been putting across the country, namely that they are going to pass a number of very controversial and complex pieces of legislation. If the government has no intention of passing them, then I do not see why we cannot make some arrangements along the line I have suggested.

If this is the case, Mr. Speaker, then for God's sake let us make these arrangements in public, so that everyone will know about them and be able to co-operate. Sometimes members are asked for their co-operation and they do not know why. If we had given up one day's debate on the throne speech, what difference would it have made?
If further legislation is added and we continue into July, then anyone who has been here any length of time knows that if we go beyond July 1, which is an obvious cut-off date, we go on and on.

I think the government also have an obligation to tell the Canadian people, particularly members of parliament and members of the Senate, what arrangements will be made about the royal visit. I am quite sure that the royal visit will not involve an address to parliament. If it does not, then there is really no reason for parliament to be in session. It is my understanding, though this is not the information given publicly to the press, that the Queen will address her loyal subjects on the lawn of Parliament Hill and that members of the House of Commons and members of the Senate will be special guests in attendance. If this is the case, then I do not think it is necessary for parliament to sit beyond June 30.

Whether or not this is the case, Mr. Speaker, I hope that collectively we will have enough intelligence to see to it that at least one week before Christmas we will prorogue this session so that we can start a new one, not the third week in January but directly after January 1. We should debate the throne speech, bring in the estimates and the budget and then adjourn for a summer recess so that members have an opportunity to visit their constituencies to do some work.
I used the unfortunate expression ""holiday"". I thought about that word the other day when I was so tired I decided to stay in bed, and I stayed in bed until two o'clock in the

afternoon. I wondered afterwards why I was so tired. I go home at week ends and the phone starts ringing at seven o'clock in the morning, and I am sure this is the case with other hon. members. I attend several meetings during the course of the day. I have a continual round of meetings, consultations and visits, and I deal with other matters that require attention. By the time I leave for Ottawa I have not even had a week end break, but have been working seven days a week. We do have an obligation to see our constituents, Mr. Speaker; otherwise we get so far out of touch with them that we are not really representative of them.

I suppose that what I have said will fall on deaf ears-it has before. However, I hope that if we are really going to make some changes they will be made out in the open and that all members will be asked for their co-operation, instead of four or five people getting together in the back room. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said he intended to do something about improving the operations of parliament, and it seems to me that now is a good time to do it. It also seems to me that members of parliament have a special obligation this year to their constituents. Although it will be no holiday for them this year, an obligation does fall on each and every member to join in in some of the centennial activities in their ridings for which their constituents have worked so very hard, and in which I am sure they would like to see their member participate.

If time allows I hope the Prime Minister will make some statement as to what improvements he wants and what our timetable will be. Then and only then can he honestly ask for the co-operation of members of parliament in the accomplishment of what is a reasonable and practical proposition.
